facts.text: Salvador was Brazil's first capital, running the colony from 1549 until the seat of government moved to Rio in 1763.
Salvador's Elevador Lacerda, an art deco public lift from 1873, still carries thousands of people a day between the upper and lower city.
Rio's Christ the Redeemer statue was voted one of the New Seven Wonders of the World in 2007.
Rio's Maracana stadium drew an estimated 200,000 spectators for the 1950 World Cup final, still the largest crowd ever at a football match.
In 2016 Rio de Janeiro became the first South American city ever to host the Olympic Games.
São Paulo is home to the largest Japanese community outside Japan, centred on the Liberdade district.
Brasília was built from scratch in under four years and inaugurated as Brazil's capital in 1960, laid out in the shape of an airplane.
Recife is nicknamed the Venice of Brazil for the rivers and dozens of bridges that stitch the city together.
Belo Horizonte's lakeside Pampulha district, designed by Oscar Niemeyer in the 1940s, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
The gold-rush town of Ouro Preto was the first place in Brazil added to the UNESCO World Heritage list, back in 1980.
Uberlândia is the second-most-populous city in the state of Minas Gerais and a major crossroads of Brazil's inland freight routes.
Ilhéus, the old cocoa capital of Brazil, is the setting of Jorge Amado's novel Gabriela, Clove and Cinnamon.
Porto Seguro is where Pedro Álvares Cabral's Portuguese fleet made landfall in 1500, the first recorded European arrival in Brazil.
Niterói's saucer-shaped Museum of Contemporary Art, perched above Guanabara Bay, was designed by Oscar Niemeyer.
Campinas hosts the University of Campinas, one of Latin America's leading research universities.
Santos runs the busiest seaport in Latin America — and its football club is where Pelé played for nearly two decades.
Curitiba pioneered bus rapid transit in the 1970s, a system later copied by cities all over the world.
Porto Alegre hosted the first World Social Forum in 2001 and is the heart of Brazil's gaucho culture.
Florianópolis sits mostly on an island, joined to the mainland by the Hercílio Luz suspension bridge, a symbol of the city since 1926.
Fortaleza's fishermen still sail jangadas, the traditional wooden rafts that have worked the Ceará coast for centuries.
Just outside Natal grows the Cashew of Pirangi, a single tree sprawling over roughly 8,500 square metres — about the size of a city block.
Belém's Círio de Nazaré procession draws well over a million people every October, one of the largest religious gatherings in the world.
Manaus built a lavish opera house, the Teatro Amazonas, deep in the rainforest during the 1890s rubber boom.
A monument in Cuiabá marks a calculated geographic centre of South America.
Campo Grande is nicknamed Cidade Morena after the red-brown earth it is built on, and serves as a gateway to the Pantanal wetlands.
Tel Aviv's White City holds over 4,000 Bauhaus-style buildings, the largest such collection in the world and a UNESCO site.
Tel Aviv was founded in 1909 on sand dunes outside the ancient port of Jaffa, which it later absorbed.
Haifa's terraced Bahá'í Gardens climb Mount Carmel in 19 landscaped steps and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Jerusalem's Old City walls standing today were built by the Ottoman sultan Suleiman the Magnificent in the 1500s.
Jerusalem's Old City packs sites sacred to Judaism, Christianity and Islam into less than one square kilometre.
Eilat, Israel's southernmost city, sits on the Red Sea beside coral reefs at the edge of the Negev desert.
Venice is built across 118 small islands laced together by around 400 bridges, with boats doing the work of cars.
The Venice Film Festival, founded in 1932, is the oldest film festival in the world.
Venetian gondolas are deliberately built lopsided, with a curved left side to balance a gondolier rowing on one side only.
Milan's Duomo took nearly six centuries to finish, from 1386 to its final touches in the 1960s.
Milan's Santa Maria delle Grazie holds Leonardo da Vinci's The Last Supper, painted on the refectory wall in the 1490s.
Milano hosts the Salone del Mobile, the largest furniture and design fair in the world.
Visitors throw roughly 1.5 million euros into Rome's Trevi Fountain each year, and the coins go to charity.
Rome's Pantheon, nearly 1,900 years old, still has the largest unreinforced concrete dome ever built.
Roma wraps entirely around Vatican City, the smallest sovereign state in the world.
Bologna's university, founded in 1088, is the oldest university in continuous operation anywhere.
Bologna's medieval porticoes run for some 60 kilometres and are listed by UNESCO.
Naples gave the world the pizza margherita, by tradition created in 1889 and named for Italy's queen.
Napoli lives in the shadow of Vesuvius, the volcano whose eruption in 79 AD buried nearby Pompeii.
Turin was united Italy's first capital in 1861, and its old Fiat Lingotto factory has a test track on the roof.
Bergamo's hilltop upper town is ringed by Venetian defensive walls that now hold UNESCO World Heritage status.
Como has been a silk-making centre since the 1500s and still produces much of Europe's high-end silk.
Verona's Roman arena, built in the first century, still stages open-air opera for thousands every summer.
Padova's botanical garden, planted in 1545 for the university where Galileo taught, is the world's oldest still in its original location.
Modena's traditional balsamic vinegar must age in wooden barrels for at least 12 years before it can carry the name.
Parma gave its name to both Parmigiano Reggiano cheese and Parma ham, and was named a UNESCO Creative City of Gastronomy.
Siena's bareback Palio horse race has been run around the shell-shaped Piazza del Campo since the Middle Ages, twice each summer.
Pisa's famous tower began leaning during construction in the 1170s because it was built on soft ground.
Firenze's cathedral is crowned by Brunelleschi's dome, still the largest masonry dome ever built.
Tiny Amalfi was once a medieval maritime republic that rivalled Venice, Pisa and Genoa for Mediterranean trade.
Sorrento's clifftop lemon groves supply the fruit behind limoncello, the region's signature liqueur.
Taormina's ancient Greek theatre frames a natural backdrop of Mount Etna and the sea.
Lecce is called the Florence of the South for the exuberant baroque carving of its soft local limestone.
Catania was rebuilt in baroque style out of black volcanic stone after Mount Etna and an earthquake devastated it in the 1600s.
Bari's basilica has held the relics of St Nicholas — the original Santa Claus — since sailors brought them there in 1087.
Palermo's Teatro Massimo is the largest opera house in Italy, with an auditorium famed for near-perfect acoustics.
Tivoli holds two UNESCO sites within one small town: Hadrian's sprawling Roman villa and the fountain gardens of Villa d'Este.
Istanbul is the only major city in the world that spans two continents, straddling Europe and Asia across the Bosphorus.
Istanbul's Grand Bazaar, trading since the 1450s, covers over 60 streets and some 4,000 shops.
Ankara replaced Istanbul as Turkey's capital in 1923, and the soft-haired angora goat takes its name from the city.
Antalya regularly ranks among the world's most visited cities, and Roman emperor Hadrian's marble gate still marks the old town entrance.
Izmir, the ancient Greek city of Smyrna, is one of several places that claim to be the birthplace of Homer.
Bucharest's Palace of the Parliament is listed by Guinness World Records as the heaviest building on Earth.
Brasov's Black Church is the largest Gothic church between Vienna and Istanbul, and Bran Castle of Dracula fame sits just outside town.
Cluj, the unofficial capital of Transylvania, hosts Untold, one of the biggest electronic music festivals in Europe.
Arthur Guinness signed a 9,000-year lease on Dublin's St James's Gate brewery in 1759, and the beer is still brewed there.
Dublin's Trinity College displays the Book of Kells, an illuminated gospel manuscript created around 800 AD.
Cork's English Market has been feeding the city from the same spot since 1788.
Berlin has more bridges than Venice — around 1,700 of them cross its rivers and canals.
The Berlin Wall stood for 28 years and fell in November 1989; a double row of cobblestones now traces its path through the city.
Munich's Oktoberfest began in 1810 as the public party for a Bavarian royal wedding and never really stopped.
Munich's Englischer Garten is larger than New York's Central Park and has a standing river wave that is surfed year-round.
München enforced the 1516 Reinheitsgebot beer purity law, which allowed only water, barley and hops in the brew.
Frankfurt is home to the European Central Bank and a skyline of towers that earned it the nickname Mainhattan.
The Frankfurt Book Fair, with roots in the 15th century, is the largest book fair in the world.
Hamburg counts roughly 2,500 bridges, more than Venice and Amsterdam combined.
Cologne Cathedral took 632 years to complete, and on its completion in 1880 it was briefly the tallest building in the world.
Köln's carnival season officially opens on the 11th of November at exactly 11:11 in the morning.
Stuttgart is the home of both Mercedes-Benz and Porsche, each with its own museum in the city.
Wolfsburg was founded in 1938 to house Volkswagen workers, and its plant remains one of the largest car factories in the world.
Düsseldorf hosts the largest Japanese community in Germany, complete with its own annual Japan Day festival.
Dortmund's Yellow Wall, the south stand of its football stadium, holds nearly 25,000 fans — the biggest standing terrace in European football.
A bronze statue of the Town Musicians of Bremen — donkey, dog, cat and rooster from the Grimm tale — stands beside the city hall.
Lübeck, medieval queen of the Hanseatic League, was among the first city ensembles in Germany to be listed by UNESCO, and is famous for marzipan.
Rostock's university, founded in 1419, is the oldest in the Baltic region.
Schwerin's fairytale castle sits on its own island in a lake and houses the state parliament of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.
Johann Sebastian Bach led the St Thomas Choir in Leipzig for 27 years, and the city's Monday demonstrations helped bring down the Berlin Wall.
Dresden's Frauenkirche lay in ruins for half a century after 1945 and was rebuilt using thousands of its original stones, reopening in 2005.
Chemnitz is watched over by a seven-metre bronze head of Karl Marx and holds the title of European Capital of Culture 2025.
Potsdam's Babelsberg studio, opened in 1912, is the oldest large-scale film studio in the world.
Kassel stages documenta, one of the world's most important contemporary art exhibitions, once every five years.
Dostoevsky's losses at the Wiesbaden casino tables helped inspire his novel The Gambler.
Heidelberg's university, founded in 1386, is the oldest in Germany, and the old town survived the Second World War almost untouched.
Freiburg's streets are lined with little water channels called Bächle — local legend says stepping in one means you will marry a Freiburger.
Augsburg's Fuggerei, founded in 1521, is the world's oldest social housing complex still in use, with annual rent below one euro.
Germany's first railway ran from Nürnberg in 1835, and the city's Christkindlesmarkt is among the oldest Christmas markets anywhere.
The London Underground, opened in 1863, is the oldest metro system in the world.
Big Ben is the name of the bell, not the tower — the tower itself was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012.
London's black-cab drivers must pass The Knowledge, memorising some 25,000 streets, which typically takes years.
The world's first inter-city passenger railway opened between Manchester and Liverpool in 1830.
The first stored-program computer, nicknamed the Baby, ran its first program at the University of Manchester in 1948.
Liverpool's Hope Street links the city's two cathedrals — one Anglican, one Catholic — at either end.
The Beatles played nearly 300 gigs at Liverpool's Cavern Club before conquering the world.
Birmingham, England, has more canals by length than Venice, dug to move goods during the Industrial Revolution.
The Cadbury family built the model village of Bournville around their chocolate factory on the edge of Birmingham.
Glasgow's Clyde shipyards built some of the most famous liners afloat, including the Queen Mary and the QE2.
Members and alumni of Cambridge's university have won well over a hundred Nobel Prizes — more than most countries.
Edinburgh Castle sits on the plug of an extinct volcano, and the city's Fringe is the largest arts festival in the world.
A century ago Cardiff shipped more coal than any port on Earth; today its Principality Stadium has a fully retractable roof.
Swansea is the birthplace of the poet Dylan Thomas, and the nearby Gower Peninsula was the UK's first Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty.
Wrexham's football club, founded in 1864, is among the oldest professional clubs in the world — and is now owned by two Hollywood actors.
The Titanic was built in Belfast's Harland and Wolff shipyard, whose giant yellow cranes still dominate the skyline.
Derry is the only completely walled city in Ireland, and its 17th-century walls were never breached — hence the nickname Maiden City.
Dundee built the Antarctic research ship RRS Discovery and became the UK's first UNESCO City of Design.
Stoke-on-Trent is a federation of six towns whose kilns fired Wedgwood and Spode china, earning it the name The Potteries.
Sunderland once launched more ships than any other town in the world, and today builds more cars than anywhere else in Britain.
Durham's Norman cathedral, begun in 1093, forms a UNESCO World Heritage Site together with the castle beside it.
The KitKat was invented at Rowntree's factory in York, a city still ringed by England's most complete medieval walls.
Stainless steel was developed in Sheffield by Harry Brearley in 1913, sealing the city's reputation for cutlery.
Nottingham's Ye Olde Trip to Jerusalem, carved into the castle rock, claims to have been serving ale since 1189.
The oldest surviving moving-picture footage was shot on Leeds Bridge by Louis Le Prince in 1888.
Newcastle's Tyne Bridge was built by the same firm as the Sydney Harbour Bridge, and the two are near-identical in silhouette.
Brighton's seafront runs the world's oldest operating electric railway, opened by Magnus Volk in 1883.
Blackpool Tower, opened in 1894, was directly inspired by the Eiffel Tower, and the town's Illuminations have shone since 1879.
The Eiffel Tower was meant to stand for just 20 years after the 1889 World's Fair — its use as a radio mast saved it.
The Louvre in Paris is the most visited museum in the world, welcoming millions more visitors than any rival.
The Lumière brothers shot some of the first films ever made in Lyon and premiered their cinematograph in 1895.
Lyon's old town hides traboules, covered passageways once used by silk workers to move cloth between streets.
Toulouse is called the Pink City for its rose-coloured brick, and final assembly of Airbus airliners happens there.
Marseille is France's oldest city, founded by Greek sailors around 600 BC.
Nice's Promenade des Anglais is named after the English visitors who paid for the seafront walkway in the 1820s.
Lille's Braderie, held every September, is the largest flea market in Europe.
Amiens Cathedral is the largest Gothic cathedral in France by volume, and Jules Verne wrote many of his novels while living in the city.
The kings of France were crowned in Reims Cathedral for over a thousand years, and millions of champagne bottles age in chalk cellars beneath the city.
Colmar, the Little Venice of Alsace, is the birthplace of Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi, sculptor of the Statue of Liberty.
Strasbourg Cathedral was the tallest building in the world for over two centuries, and the city hosts the European Parliament.
Grenoble hosted the 1968 Winter Olympics and runs one of the world's oldest urban cable cars up to its Bastille fortress.
Annecy's alpine lake is fed by mountain springs and is often described as the cleanest lake in Europe.
Bordeaux's riverfront, the Port of the Moon, is one of the largest urban areas ever inscribed by UNESCO.
Surfing arrived in Europe at Biarritz in the 1950s, in a resort made fashionable a century earlier by Napoleon III.
Two medieval towers still guard the harbour mouth of La Rochelle, once one of France's great Atlantic ports.
Brest has been the home of the French Atlantic fleet since Cardinal Richelieu chose its sheltered harbour in the 1600s.
Quimper has produced its hand-painted faience pottery since 1690.
Rennes holds the Marché des Lices every Saturday, one of the biggest food markets in France, beneath half-timbered medieval houses.
Salvador Dalí famously declared Perpignan's railway station the centre of the universe, and the city keeps a proudly Catalan identity.
Montpellier's medical school has taught continuously since around 1220, longer than any other in the world.
The Palace of Versailles has about 2,300 rooms, and the treaty ending the First World War was signed in its Hall of Mirrors.
Cannes has hosted its film festival since 1946, turning a fishing village promenade into the world's most photographed red carpet.
Madrid's Restaurante Botín, open since 1725, holds the Guinness record as the oldest restaurant in the world.
All road distances in Spain are measured from Kilometre Zero, a plaque in Madrid's Puerta del Sol.
Barcelona's Sagrada Família has been under construction since 1882 and is still not finished.
Barcelona's Eixample district was laid out in the 1850s as a vast grid of chamfered octagonal blocks, decades ahead of its time.
Valencia is the birthplace of paella, and a 9-kilometre park now winds through the dry riverbed where the Turia once flowed.
Sevilla's cathedral is the largest Gothic cathedral in the world, and Magellan's circumnavigation expedition set out from the city in 1519.
Granada's Alhambra palace complex is Spain's most visited monument, and many of the city's bars still serve a free tapa with every drink.
Pablo Picasso was born in Málaga in 1881, in a city founded by the Phoenicians nearly 3,000 years ago.
The Guggenheim museum, opened in 1997, so transformed Bilbao's fortunes that urban planners now speak of the Bilbao effect.
San Sebastián has one of the highest concentrations of Michelin stars per resident of any city in the world.
Vitoria-Gasteiz, seat of the Basque government, was named European Green Capital in 2012 for the ring of parks encircling it.
A Coruña's Tower of Hercules is the oldest Roman lighthouse still in use, guiding ships for nearly 2,000 years.
Vigo lands more fish for human consumption than any other port in Europe.
Santiago de Compostela is the endpoint of the Camino pilgrimage routes, and its cathedral swings a giant incense burner over the crowds.
Girona's cathedral has the widest Gothic nave in the world, and its old streets stood in for King's Landing in Game of Thrones.
Tarragona's Roman amphitheatre sits right on the seashore, part of the UNESCO-listed remains of ancient Tarraco.
Alicante is watched over by Santa Bárbara castle on Mount Benacantil, and its beaches blaze with bonfires every San Juan midsummer night.
Elche is surrounded by more than 200,000 palm trees, Europe's largest palm grove and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Burgos Cathedral is a UNESCO site in its own right, and the medieval warlord El Cid is buried beneath its crossing.
León's cathedral holds around 1,800 square metres of medieval stained glass, among the finest ensembles in Europe.
Salamanca's university, founded in 1218, is the oldest in Spain — students still hunt for the lucky frog carved on its facade.
Cáceres' walled old town blends Roman, Moorish and Gothic building so completely that UNESCO listed the whole ensemble.
Mérida's Roman theatre, built around 15 BC, still hosts a classical drama festival every summer.
Alcalá de Henares is the birthplace of Cervantes, and its 1499 university gave UNESCO one of its first listed campus towns.
The New York subway has 472 stations, more than any other metro system in the world.
Around 800 languages are spoken in New York, making it the most linguistically diverse city on Earth.
New York's Central Park was the first major landscaped public park in the United States, opened in the 1850s.
George Washington was sworn in as the first US president in New York City, the country's original capital.
The Hollywood sign originally read Hollywoodland when it went up in 1923 to advertise a housing development.
Los Angeles was founded in 1781 by 44 settlers, under a Spanish name so long it filled a whole line of the founding record.
San Francisco's Golden Gate Bridge had the longest suspension span in the world from 1937 until 1964.
San Francisco's cable cars are the only moving US National Historic Landmark.
Chicago built the world's first skyscraper, the ten-storey Home Insurance Building, in 1885.
Chicago reversed the flow of its river in 1900 to protect the city's drinking water in Lake Michigan.
Boston Common, set aside in 1634, is the oldest public park in the United States, and the Boston Marathon is the world's oldest annual marathon.
The first Starbucks opened at Seattle's Pike Place Market in 1971 and still trades there.
Berry Gordy founded Motown in Detroit in 1959, and the first mile of concrete highway in America was laid on the city's Woodward Avenue.
Cleveland installed the world's first electric traffic signal in 1914 and hosts the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.
Denver is nicknamed the Mile High City because one step of the State Capitol sits exactly 5,280 feet above sea level.
Las Vegas has more hotel rooms than any other city on Earth — roughly 150,000 of them.
Phoenix records more hours of sunshine than almost any major city in the world.
Albuquerque's International Balloon Fiesta lifts hundreds of hot-air balloons at once, the largest ballooning event in the world.
Tucson was the first city in the United States to be named a UNESCO City of Gastronomy, honouring 4,000 years of desert agriculture.
San Antonio's Alamo mission, besieged in 1836, is the most visited historic site in Texas.
The frozen margarita machine was invented in Dallas in 1971 — the prototype now belongs to the Smithsonian.
Austin's official motto is the Live Music Capital of the World, and the bat colony under its Congress Avenue Bridge is North America's largest urban one.
Elvis Presley's Graceland in Memphis draws around 600,000 visitors a year, among the most visited private homes in America.
The Gateway Arch in St. Louis stands 630 feet tall, the tallest man-made monument in the United States.
Kansas City claims more fountains than any city in the world except Rome.
Omaha is home town and lifelong base of investor Warren Buffett, the Oracle of Omaha.
Salt Lake City hosted the 2002 Winter Olympics and will host them again in 2034.
San Diego's Balboa Park is larger than Central Park and hosts a zoo that pioneered open-air, cageless enclosures.
Toronto's CN Tower was the tallest free-standing structure in the world for over three decades after opening in 1976.
Roughly half of Toronto's residents were born outside Canada, making it one of the most multicultural cities anywhere.
Montreal is the largest French-speaking city in the world after Paris.
Mount Royal, the hill that gave Montréal its name, was landscaped by Frederick Law Olmsted, co-designer of Central Park.
Vancouver's Stanley Park is about ten percent bigger than New York's Central Park and is ringed by a nine-kilometre seawall.
In winter Ottawa's Rideau Canal becomes the world's largest skating rink, nearly eight kilometres long.
Quebec City is the only walled city north of Mexico whose fortifications still stand complete.
Québec City's Château Frontenac is often called the most photographed hotel in the world.
The Calgary Stampede, running since 1912, bills itself as the Greatest Outdoor Show on Earth.
West Edmonton Mall is the largest shopping centre in North America, complete with an indoor water park and skating rink.
Winnie-the-Pooh is named after a bear called Winnie — herself named for Winnipeg by the Canadian soldier who bought her.
Every Royal Canadian Mounted Police officer trains at the Depot academy in Regina, as they have since 1885.
Saskatoon is named after a local berry, and its riverbank skyline has earned it the nickname Paris of the Prairies.
Banff was Canada's first national park, created in 1885 around hot springs discovered by railway workers.
Kelowna anchors the Okanagan Valley wine country — and its lake comes with a resident monster legend, the Ogopogo.
Victoria's famous Butchart Gardens were planted in the early 1900s inside an exhausted limestone quarry.
The 1917 Halifax Harbour explosion was the largest man-made blast before the atomic bomb.
Charlottetown hosted the 1864 conference that led to Canadian Confederation, earning it the title Birthplace of Confederation.
Moncton sits near the Bay of Fundy, whose tides — the highest in the world — push a bore wave up the city's river twice a day.
On Signal Hill above St. John's, Marconi received the first transatlantic wireless signal in 1901.
Corner Brook grew around a paper mill opened in 1925, and Captain James Cook surveyed its Bay of Islands in the 1760s.
Trois-Rivières, founded in 1634, is the second-oldest city of New France after Quebec City.
Iqaluit became Canada's newest capital in 1999 and is the only one with no road or rail link to the rest of the country.
Yellowknife sits on Great Slave Lake, the deepest lake in North America, under some of the world's most reliable aurora skies.
Whitehorse is named for rapids on the Yukon River that reminded gold-rush stampeders of white horses' manes.
Beijing's Forbidden City is the largest palace complex in the world, with close to 9,000 rooms.
Beijing is the only city ever to host both the Summer and the Winter Olympic Games.
Shanghai runs the world's first commercial maglev train, covering 30 kilometres to the airport in about seven minutes.
The Port of Shanghai has been the busiest container port in the world every year since 2010.
Shenzhen grew from a town of about 30,000 people into a metropolis of over 12 million in four decades after becoming China's first special economic zone.
Shenzhen was the first major city in the world to electrify its entire bus fleet — more than 16,000 vehicles.
Guangzhou has hosted the Canton Fair, China's largest trade fair, twice a year since 1957.
Chengdu is home to the famous giant panda research base and was Asia's first UNESCO City of Gastronomy.
In Chongqing a metro line runs straight through the middle of a 19-storey residential building.
Wuhan sits where the Han meets the Yangtze, and the first bridge ever to span the Yangtze opened there in 1957.
Tombs at Mawangdui in Changsha preserved a 2,000-year-old noblewoman so well that her skin was still soft when excavated.
The 1927 Nanchang uprising is celebrated as the founding moment of the People's Liberation Army.
Zhengzhou stands on the Yellow River where the Shang dynasty built a walled capital about 3,600 years ago.
Lanzhou is the home of hand-pulled beef noodle soup, and the first permanent bridge over the Yellow River opened there in 1909.
Farmers digging a well near Xi'an in 1974 uncovered the Terracotta Army — some 8,000 clay soldiers guarding China's first emperor.
Kashgar has been a Silk Road oasis for 2,000 years, and its Sunday bazaar remains one of Central Asia's largest markets.
Urumqi is the most landlocked major city in the world, about 2,500 kilometres from the nearest coastline.
Kunming is called the Spring City for its mild year-round climate and hosts Asia's largest flower market.
Harbin's winter Ice and Snow Festival builds a full-scale illuminated city out of river ice every year.
Changchun built China's first automobile plant in the 1950s and is still called the cradle of the Chinese car industry.
Shenyang's Mukden Palace is the only imperial palace complex in China outside Beijing, built by the early Qing emperors.
Nanjing's Ming-era city wall is the longest surviving city wall in the world, once stretching 35 kilometres.
Marco Polo described Hangzhou as the finest and most splendid city in the world, and its West Lake is now a UNESCO site.
Suzhou's classical gardens, refined over a thousand years, are collectively listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Zhuhai anchors one end of the 55-kilometre Hong Kong-Zhuhai-Macau bridge, the longest sea crossing ever built.
Tokyo holds more Michelin stars than any other city in the world.
Tokyo's Shinjuku is certified by Guinness as the busiest railway station on Earth, handling over three million passengers a day.
Japan's first railway opened in 1872 between Tokyo and Yokohama, and the city hosts Japan's largest Chinatown.
Osaka is nicknamed the nation's kitchen and gave Japan both takoyaki and the word kuidaore — eating yourself broke.
Kyoto served as Japan's capital for over a thousand years and still counts around 2,000 temples and shrines.
Nintendo was founded in Kyoto in 1889 — as a maker of hand-painted playing cards.
Authentic Kobe beef must come from Tajima cattle born and raised in Hyogo prefecture, of which Kobe is the capital.
Nagoya's castle is crowned by two golden shachihoko — tiger-headed fish — and Toyota's headquarters sit just outside the city.
Sapporo hosted the 1972 Winter Games — the first in Asia — and its Snow Festival carves whole palaces from packed snow.
Hakodate was among the first Japanese ports opened to foreign trade in the 1850s, and its mountain-top night view is nationally famous.
Otaru's gas-lit canal district, built for the herring trade, now houses glassblowing studios and music-box workshops.
Aomori grows more than half of Japan's apples and parades giant illuminated floats at its Nebuta festival every August.
Sendai was founded by the one-eyed samurai lord Date Masamune in 1601 and stages Japan's largest Tanabata star festival.
Morioka is famous for wanko soba, a contest-style meal where servers refill your bowl with bite-sized noodles until you beg them to stop.
Kanazawa produces about 99 percent of Japan's gold leaf and escaped wartime bombing, keeping its samurai and geisha districts intact.
Nagano hosted the 1998 Winter Olympics and grew around Zenko-ji, a temple founded in the 7th century.
Hiroshima's Genbaku Dome was left standing as a peace memorial, and the city is Japan's biggest oyster producer.
Okayama is the legendary home of Momotaro the Peach Boy, and its Koraku-en ranks among Japan's three great gardens.
Matsue's black castle is one of only a dozen in Japan with its original wooden keep, and writer Lafcadio Hearn made the city his home.
Matsuyama's Dogo Onsen has offered hot-spring bathing for around 3,000 years, making it one of Japan's oldest baths.
Takamatsu's Ritsurin Garden took feudal lords a century to complete and is the gateway to the sanuki udon heartland.
Fukuoka is the birthplace of tonkotsu ramen and keeps Japan's largest concentration of yatai street-food stalls.
Kagoshima faces Sakurajima, one of the world's most active volcanoes, which regularly dusts the city with ash.
Naha was the capital of the independent Ryukyu Kingdom for centuries before Okinawa became part of Japan.
Mumbai's dabbawalas deliver around 200,000 home-cooked lunches a day with an error rate so low it is studied by business schools.
Mumbai's Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus is a working railway station so ornate it is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
New Delhi was designed by Edwin Lutyens and inaugurated in 1931 after the capital moved from Calcutta.
New Delhi's India Gate bears the names of over 13,000 soldiers of the Indian Army who fell in the First World War.
Bengaluru is called the Silicon Valley of India, and its Lalbagh garden grew from a royal Mughal-style garden of the 1760s.
Chennai's Marina Beach stretches about 13 kilometres, one of the longest urban beaches in the world.
Kolkata has run trams since 1902, the oldest operating tram network in Asia.
Jaipur was painted pink in 1876 to welcome the Prince of Wales, and the colour is still protected by law in the old city.
Jodhpur's indigo-washed old town spreads below Mehrangarh Fort — and the city gave its name to jodhpur riding trousers.
Udaipur is the City of Lakes, where the Lake Palace appears to float on the waters of Lake Pichola.
Some 20,000 workers spent about 22 years building the Taj Mahal in Agra, finishing around 1653.
Varanasi is among the oldest continuously inhabited cities on Earth, its riverfront stepped with nearly 90 ghats.
Lucknow's Bara Imambara contains one of the largest arched halls in the world, built without a single supporting beam.
Patna stands on the site of ancient Pataliputra, capital of the Maurya empire under Ashoka the Great.
Shillong is nicknamed the Scotland of the East for its rolling hills, and is celebrated as India's rock music capital.
Guwahati sits on the Brahmaputra, a river that swells to around 10 kilometres wide near the city in monsoon flood.
Bhubaneswar is called the Temple City — medieval chronicles counted hundreds of stone temples, and dozens still stand.
Visakhapatnam turned a real submarine, INS Kursura, into South Asia's first submarine museum on its beach.
Roughly 90 percent of the world's diamonds are cut and polished in Surat.
Vadodara's Laxmi Vilas Palace is about four times the floor area of Buckingham Palace and is still a royal residence.
Ahmedabad became India's first UNESCO World Heritage City in 2017, and Gandhi ran his Sabarmati Ashram there for 13 years.
During Dasara, Mysuru Palace is lit by nearly 100,000 bulbs, a tradition of the city's 400-year-old royal festival.
Mangaluru's clay roof tiles were such a successful export in the 1800s that Mangalore tiles still roof buildings across Asia.
Coimbatore is called the Manchester of South India for its textile mills, and the 34-metre Adiyogi statue nearby is the world's largest bust.
Madurai's Meenakshi Temple raises 14 towered gateways covered in thousands of painted sculptures, and its jasmine holds protected GI status.
Hyderabad's Golconda mines produced legendary diamonds including the Koh-i-Noor, centuries before the city became a tech hub.
Pune is called the Oxford of the East for its universities, and the Aga Khan Palace there held Gandhi prisoner in the 1940s.
Nagpur's Zero Mile marker was the point from which British India measured its distances, and the city is famous for its oranges.
Gurugram grew from farmland into one of India's biggest corporate hubs in barely three decades.
Noida, planned in 1976, hosts one of India's largest film studio complexes and had a Formula 1 circuit on its doorstep.
The roof of the Sydney Opera House is covered in more than a million self-cleaning ceramic tiles.
Sydney Harbour Bridge is nicknamed the Coathanger, and climbers have been walking over its arch since 1998.
Melbourne runs the largest tram network in the world, about 250 kilometres of track.
Brisbane will host the 2032 Olympic Games, the third time Australia has won the Games.
The Gold Coast unrolls about 57 kilometres of surf beaches, including the break that named Surfers Paradise.
Cairns is the gateway to the Great Barrier Reef, the largest living structure on Earth.
Perth is often called the most isolated major city in the world — its nearest big neighbour is over 2,000 kilometres away.
Fremantle hosted the 1987 America's Cup defence, and its convict-built prison is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
Kalgoorlie's Super Pit gold mine grew so large it could be seen from space — roughly 3.5 kilometres long and 600 metres deep.
Adelaide was planned in 1836 as a grid wrapped entirely in parkland, and its Fringe is the largest arts festival in the Southern Hemisphere.
Alice Springs pioneered the School of the Air in 1951, teaching outback children by radio across an area bigger than many countries.
In the opal town of Coober Pedy, many residents live underground in dugouts to escape the desert heat.
Mount Gambier's Blue Lake, filling a volcanic crater, turns a vivid cobalt blue every summer and back to grey in winter.
Darwin sits closer to Jakarta than to Sydney, and was rebuilt twice — after wartime bombing in 1942 and Cyclone Tracy in 1974.
Hobart, founded in 1804, is Australia's second-oldest capital and the finish line of the Sydney to Hobart yacht race.
Launceston's Cataract Gorge puts a wilderness reserve, chairlift included, ten minutes' walk from the city centre.
Devonport is the home port of the Spirit of Tasmania ferries that link the island to the Australian mainland.
Canberra was designed from scratch by Chicago architects Walter and Marion Griffin, winners of a 1912 competition.
Belconnen was laid out in the 1960s as one of Canberra's planned satellite town centres, wrapped around Lake Ginninderra.
Gungahlin is Canberra's youngest district, connected to the city by light rail in 2019.
The lighthouse at Byron Bay stands on Cape Byron, the easternmost point of the Australian mainland.
Geelong grew rich on the wool trade and is home to the Cats, one of the oldest football clubs in the world, founded in 1859.
Ballarat's Eureka Stockade rebellion of 1854 became a defining moment in Australian democracy during the gold rush.
Birmingham, Alabama, is watched over by Vulcan — the largest cast-iron statue in the world.

tips: Passing on a street does not kill it — it goes straight to auction, where you can sometimes win it back below the sticker price.
Auctions are the only place streets sell below list price, so a table full of cautious players is a table full of bargains.
Auction bids rise in steps of at least $10, and every new bid resets the countdown, so a late bid keeps maximum pressure on.
Your leading auction bid leaves your cash immediately and is refunded only if you are outbid — do not count on spending that money twice.
Bidding a rival up at auction is sweet until they pass — the escrow means you must be able to pay whatever number you shouted.
If nobody bids at all, the street stays with the bank, so a cheap opening bid can steal a tile the table ignored.
When someone goes bankrupt to the bank, their streets return to the open market — a second chance at the colour you missed.
Bankrupting to a player hands them everything you own, so if the end is coming, mind who your last debt is owed to.
Mortgaging pays half the printed price and costs that half plus 10 percent to lift — cheap credit when it finishes a set.
A mortgaged street collects nothing, so mortgage your loose single streets and never the set that is doing the earning.
You cannot mortgage a street while its colour has houses anywhere — the buildings have to be sold off first.
Selling a house refunds only half of what it cost, so build with money you will not need back in a hurry.
Keep a cash cushion: a rent you cannot cover drops you into the debt phase, where everything you sell goes at the worst prices.
When you are in debt, you choose what gets mortgaged or sold — sacrifice the loose ends and protect the earning set.
The Earnings Tax takes 10 percent of your cash on hand, so a huge unspent pile is itself a liability; the Premium Tax is a flat $75 however rich you are.
Early in the game, pay the $50 prison fine at once — every turn in a cell is a turn your rivals spend buying streets.
Late in the game a prison cell is a rent-free hotel: you still collect from your streets while locked up, unless the no-prison-rent rule is on.
With the no-prison-rent rule on, your own jail time switches your whole empire off — pay the fine and get out fast.
You cannot camp in prison forever: after three failed rolls the $50 fine is charged automatically and your roll plays out.
A double breaks you out of prison for free, but the escape roll does not earn the usual extra turn.
Rolling a double earns another roll — but a third double in one turn is a straight trip to prison, with no salary on the way.
Get-out-of-prison cards can be traded like anything else, and they are worth most to whoever keeps landing behind bars.
With even-build on, houses must stay level across the colour, so budget for the whole row rather than one favourite street.
The rent curve bends hardest at the third house — that is usually the point where a street starts repaying its buildings.
The dearest street in every colour uses a richer rent table than its neighbours, so when a set sits uneven, give it the extra house.
A hotel is simply the fifth build on a street, and there is no housing shortage here — the race is about cash, not pieces.
A street with any building on it cannot be traded at all, so sell down to bare ground before shopping a set around.
Airports pay 25, 50, 100 and then 200 as you collect the set — four of them make a tidy empire that never needs a house.
Utility rent is the victim's dice roll times four, or times ten with both — the second utility is worth far more than the first.
With the double-rent rule on, a completed colour earns twice the rent before you build anything, so sets matter even when you are broke.
A street that completes somebody's colour is worth far more than the number printed on it — price it like the weapon it is.
Owning one street of a rival's colour is a veto: they cannot build until you sell, so never let it go cheap.
Some opponents will pay close to double for the last street of their set — if you must sell a completer, hold out for the premium.
The trades most likely to be accepted swap streets from different colours so both sides walk away with a finished set.
An offer can bundle cash, streets and get-out-of-prison cards all at once — sweeten a lopsided swap with money.
You cannot promise money you do not have: trade cash is capped at what is actually in your hand.
If the board changes between offer and accept — an auction, a bankruptcy, another trade — the deal is re-checked and dies rather than executing stale.
Some players remember being refused and will not chase the same street again for a while — a firm no buys you quiet laps.
You can see who is currently reading your trade offer — if they are staring and not accepting, it may be time to sweeten it.
Head-to-head, if you can never build while your rival already has, four laps past START force one blocking street to you at 1.7 times its price — but only once every street on the board is owned.
The deadlock purchase happens only if you can pay on the spot, so bank cash while you walk those laps.
The deadlock rule never moves a mortgaged street — a mortgaged wall stays a wall, whichever side of it you are on.
Paying 1.7 times list through the deadlock rule is the expensive way out — offering your rival a fair trade first is almost always cheaper.
With three or more players the deadlock rule stays off entirely — trading is the only way through a wall.
The turn clock removes players who stall, and their streets go back to the bank, not to whoever was owed money.
Every deliberate action resets your turn clock, so a long think is fine as long as you keep doing something.
When someone disconnects, anyone can grant them extra time twice — after that it takes the whole table to keep waiting.
Landing exactly on START pays $300 instead of the usual $200 for passing it.
Vacation costs you your next turn — and with the vacation-cash rule on, whoever lands there sweeps every tax paid since the last visitor.
On a short board like Blitz the salary comes around fast, so cheap colours pay themselves off much quicker.
On Lucky Wheel half the board is cards, so swings are violent — carry a bigger cash reserve than feels natural.
The stretch just past the prison corner catches every released prisoner's next roll, which makes those streets land on far more often than the far side of the board.
Buy early and buy broadly — every street you hold is one your rivals cannot complete a colour without.
In a team game nobody pays rent to a teammate, and the team lives while any one member is solvent — keep the poorest of you afloat.
A mortgaged street can change hands in a trade, but its new owner inherits the lift cost — discount it accordingly.
With auctions switched off, a passed street simply waits for the next player to land on it — passing is a gift to whoever is right behind you.
Watch what your opponents are one street short of — the moment before someone completes a colour is your last cheap chance to stop them.
